title: Telegraphe de Chappe (Fig. 19)
creator: Unknown French engraver (book illustration)
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere. The repository that hosts it does not name the source book (see report).
original_holder: Unidentified 19th-century French book, captioned 'Fig. 19. - Telegraphe de Chappe'; scan hosted in the delocalizer/chappe GitHub repository
caption: A cutaway of a Chappe signal tower. The operator in the room below works a set of levers that swing the long regulator beam and its two short arms on the mast above, and each position of the arms stands for a code. This is a later teaching engraving, not a drawing made in the 1790s.

title: Telegraph von Claude Chappe (Fig. 1)
creator: Unknown engraver, after an illustration in Ternant, Les Telegraphes
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Michael Geistbeck, Der Weltverkehr (Freiburg: Herder, late 19th century), fig. 1
caption: The Chappe signal arm on its tower, as drawn for a German history of world communications. The book credits the drawing to the French telegraph historian A. L. Ternant. This copy is small (200 px wide).

title: The Morse register (Fig. 9)
creator: Alfred Vail (author); unknown engraver
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Alfred Vail, The American Electro Magnetic Telegraph (Philadelphia, 1845), fig. 9
caption: The receiving register used on the Washington-Baltimore line. Clockwork pulls a paper strip from the reel past a stylus, and the electromagnet presses the stylus into the paper to emboss dots and dashes. Vail, Morse's partner and the line's Baltimore operator, published this engraving a year after the line opened.

title: Morse's first telegraph instrument (Fig. 62)
creator: Unknown photographer (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Elmer Ellsworth Burns, The Story of Great Inventions (New York: Harper, 1910), fig. 62
caption: Morse's 1837 prototype, built on a painter's canvas-stretcher frame. A swinging pendulum carried a pencil that zigzagged a line onto moving paper whenever current flowed. The photograph shows the surviving instrument decades later, not a scene from 1837.

title: The first message by telegraph
creator: Unknown illustrator (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Willis Duff Piercy, Great Inventions and Discoveries (New York: Charles E. Merrill, 1911)
caption: 'What hath God wrought?' written out in Morse's code with the letters beneath. It is a later redrawing for a schoolbook, not a reproduction of the original 1844 paper tape, which is in the Library of Congress.

title: Morse and the first telegraph
creator: Unknown engraver (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Rupert S. Holland, Historic Inventions (Philadelphia: George W. Jacobs & Co., 1911)
caption: Samuel F. B. Morse in middle age, holding the wire of a register that stands beside him. It is a formal portrait made years after 1844, not a picture of the day the line opened.

title: Cooke and Wheatstone needle telegraph, Paddington station (Fig. 61)
creator: Alfred Vail (author); unknown engraver
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Alfred Vail, The American Electro Magnetic Telegraph (Philadelphia, 1845), fig. 61
caption: Vail's diagram of the British rival system at the Paddington end of the Great Western Railway line to Slough. Needles on a lettered diamond dial point to letters, and keys below select the circuits. Vail drew it to compare it with Morse's one-wire code.

title: H.M.S. Agamemnon laying the Atlantic telegraph cable in 1858. A whale crosses the line.
creator: Robert Dudley (artist); R. M. Bryson (lithographer); Day & Son
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: W. H. Russell, The Atlantic Telegraph (London: Day & Son, 1865)
caption: The British warship Agamemnon pays out cable over her stern in mid-ocean while a whale surfaces close to the line. Dudley drew the 1858 scene from accounts. He sailed with the 1865 expedition, not the 1858 one.

title: Trinity Bay, Newfoundland. Exterior view of telegraph house in 1857-1858
creator: Robert Dudley (artist); G. McCulloch (lithographer); Day & Son
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: W. H. Russell, The Atlantic Telegraph (London: Day & Son, 1865)
caption: The snowbound wooden telegraph house in Trinity Bay, where the American end of the 1858 cable came ashore and the first transatlantic messages were received.

title: Facsimile of the first public news message received through the Atlantic cable
creator: Atlantic Telegraph Company clerk (original); facsimile in Bright's book
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Charles Bright, The Story of the Atlantic Cable (New York: D. Appleton, 1903), fig. 31
caption: A message form from the Valentia station, dated 17 August 1858, giving shipping news: the Cunard ship Europa had collided with the Arabia, and no lives were lost. It is a printed facsimile of the handwritten slip, not the original form.

title: The Great Eastern under weigh, July 23rd [1865]
creator: Robert Dudley (artist); T. Picken (lithographer); Day & Son
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: W. H. Russell, The Atlantic Telegraph (London: Day & Son, 1865)
caption: The giant steamship Great Eastern leaves Valentia with the whole 1865 cable in her tanks. The caption admits that the escort ships, including HMS Terrible, were added by the artist. Dudley was on board as the expedition's artist.

title: John Watkins Brett, Charles Tilston Bright, Cyrus West Field
creator: Unknown photographers; halftone plate
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Charles Bright, The Story of the Atlantic Cable (New York: D. Appleton, 1903)
caption: The three 'projectors' of the Atlantic Telegraph Company: Brett, the cable pioneer; Bright, the engineer, who was 26 in 1858; and Field, the New York merchant who promoted it. The book's author was Bright's son.

title: A. G. Bell, Telegraphy, Patent No. 174,465 (sheet 2)
creator: Alexander Graham Bell (inventor); U.S. Patent Office
why_public_domain: Work of the U.S. federal government; public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Also published in 1876.
original_holder: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration; reproduced in OpenStax U.S. History
caption: The second drawing sheet of Bell's telephone patent. Fig. 7 at the bottom shows two cones joined by a wire: speech into one, sound out of the other. This copy is small (260 px wide).

title: First Bell telephone receiver and transmitter (Fig. 68)
creator: Unknown photographer (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Elmer Ellsworth Burns, The Story of Great Inventions (New York: Harper, 1910), fig. 68
caption: Two of Bell's earliest instruments: the conical receiver and the transmitter with its membrane. The photograph was taken years later, when the objects had become relics.

title: Liquid transmitter exhibited in Philadelphia (Fig. 19)
creator: Unknown wood engraver (signed C.L.)
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Th. du Moncel, The Telephone, the Microphone, and the Phonograph (London: Kegan Paul, English edition c. 1879), fig. 19
caption: The variable-resistance transmitter Bell showed at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition. A platinum wire fixed to the membrane dips into acidulated water, so the voice changes the current. Du Moncel quotes Bell's own description.

title: Drawing accompanying Elisha Gray's caveat (Fig. 20)
creator: Elisha Gray (design); unknown French wood engraver (signed C.L.)
why_public_domain: A 19th-century book illustration; long out of copyright everywhere.
original_holder: Th. du Moncel, The Telephone, the Microphone, and the Phonograph (London: Kegan Paul, English edition c. 1879), fig. 20
caption: Du Moncel's engraving of the drawing in Gray's caveat, filed the same day as Bell's patent application. A speaker talks into a liquid transmitter and a listener hears a receiver at the other end of the wire. Du Moncel printed it so readers could judge 'the share which should be ascribed to Mr. Elisha Gray'.

title: Marconi and his wireless-telegraph sending and receiving instruments (Fig. 108)
creator: Unknown photographer (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Elmer Ellsworth Burns, The Story of Great Inventions (New York: Harper, 1910), fig. 108
caption: Guglielmo Marconi at a table with a spark-coil transmitter and a tape-printing receiver, the kind of apparatus used in his early long-distance trials. The printed book caption is part of the scan.

title: Guglielmo Marconi
creator: Unknown photographer (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Williams, The Romance of Modern Invention (London: Seeley, 1907)
caption: Marconi in his early thirties, a few years after the Signal Hill reception of December 1901 made him world-famous.

title: Poldhu Towers, the station of the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company
creator: Unknown photographer (book illustration)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Williams, The Romance of Modern Invention (London: Seeley, 1907)
caption: The Cornwall transmitting station with its four lattice towers. The towers replaced the ring of masts that a gale wrecked in 1901, so in December 1901 the 'S' was sent from a makeshift fan aerial and not from this layout.

title: Early form of coherer (Fig. 17)
creator: Oliver Lodge (author); unknown draughtsman
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Oliver J. Lodge, Signalling across Space without Wires (3rd ed., London: The Electrician, 1900), fig. 17
caption: A spiral of thin iron wire with an adjustable contact: one of Lodge's own early detectors for Hertzian waves. Lodge demonstrated wireless signalling at Oxford in 1894, before Marconi's first patents.

title: Marconi signalling mast at Dover Town Hall (Fig. 49)
creator: Unknown photographer; first published in The Electrician
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Oliver J. Lodge, Signalling across Space without Wires (3rd ed., 1900), fig. 49, from The Electrician vol. XLIII
caption: The aerial mast rigged on Dover Town Hall for the 1899 Marconi trials. In March 1899 messages first crossed the English Channel by wireless between South Foreland and Wimereux.

title: The Titanic (photographed in Southampton Water the day she sailed)
creator: Unknown photographer
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Gracie, The Truth about the Titanic (New York: Mitchell Kennerley, 1913)
caption: The Titanic leaves Southampton on 10 April 1912. Her wireless aerial is strung between the two masts. Gracie was a survivor and used the photograph in his account.

title: S.S. Titanic: profile showing decks and watertight bulkheads
creator: U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce
why_public_domain: Work of the U.S. federal government; public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105. Printed by order of the Senate, 20 August 1912.
original_holder: U.S. Senate, Report No. 806, 'Titanic' Disaster (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1912)
caption: The profile printed in the U.S. Senate inquiry report. Letters along the bottom mark the watertight bulkheads (A to P), and the shaded forward compartments show where the sea came in. The inquiry also examined the wireless messages and set new rules for shipboard radio.

title: Captain Rostron of S.S. Carpathia
creator: Unknown photographer
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Gracie, The Truth about the Titanic (New York: Mitchell Kennerley, 1913)
caption: Arthur Rostron, who turned the Carpathia toward the Titanic's position within minutes of his wireless operator Harold Cottam taking down the distress call, and reached the lifeboats at dawn.

title: The overturned Engelhardt boat B
creator: Unknown photographer (passenger on the Carpathia)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Gracie, The Truth about the Titanic (New York: Mitchell Kennerley, 1913)
caption: A lifeboat with rowers passes the upturned canvas-sided collapsible B. Gracie and Titanic's junior wireless operator Harold Bride both survived the night on this overturned boat. Nobody is visible on it in the photograph.

title: Photographed from the Carpathia, April 15, 1912
creator: Unknown photographer (passenger on the Carpathia)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Archibald Gracie, The Truth about the Titanic (New York: Mitchell Kennerley, 1913)
caption: Two views of the open sea on the morning of the rescue, with ice on the horizon: the ice field that ships had warned the Titanic about by wireless the day before.

title: The Zimmermann telegram as sent by Western Union to Mexico City
creator: German Embassy, Washington (Bernstorff); Western Union Telegraph Company
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago). The original form is held by the U.S. National Archives.
original_holder: U.S. National Archives (General Records of the Department of State, RG 59); scan via Wikimedia Commons as credited by the hosting repository
caption: The coded text that Ambassador Bernstorff relayed from Washington to the German Legation in Mexico City, 'via Galveston', on a Western Union form dated 19 January 1917. The columns of numbers are code groups. A copy of this form, obtained from Western Union, helped the British prove the telegram was genuine without revealing that they had broken the code.

title: The Temptation
creator: Unknown cartoonist, Dallas Morning News
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Library of Congress (credited by OpenStax U.S. History)
caption: Published the day after the telegram became public. Germany, drawn as the devil, offers Mexico the lost lands of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. This copy is small (260 px wide).

title: U.S. carrier under attack during the Battle of Midway
creator: U.S. Navy photographer
why_public_domain: Work of the U.S. federal government; public domain under 17 U.S.C. 105.
original_holder: U.S. Navy / National Archives (credited by the hosting repository; Navy negative number not given there)
caption: Anti-aircraft bursts fill the sky as a burning American carrier is attacked. This matches the well-known Navy photograph of USS Yorktown hit by planes from Hiryu on the afternoon of 4 June. The hosting site's caption instead calls the ship Hiryu, but the ship is clearly American (see report).

title: ARPA Net, December 1970 (logical map)
creator: Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) for ARPA
why_public_domain: Prepared under ARPA contract and published before 1978, apparently without a copyright notice, which would make it public domain in the US. This is weaker than a federal-employee work (see report).
original_holder: Collected by Noel J. Chiappa; mirrored in the larsbrinkhoff/arpanet-map repository
caption: The network a year after the first IMPs were installed: thirteen IMP switching computers from UCLA and SRI to MIT, BBN and Harvard, with the host computers attached to each.

title: ARPANET logical map, March 1977
creator: Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) for ARPA
why_public_domain: Prepared under ARPA contract and published before 1978, apparently without a copyright notice. Wikimedia Commons lists it as public domain on that basis, which is weaker than a federal-employee work (see report).
original_holder: Bolt Beranek and Newman; scan via Wikimedia Commons as credited by the hosting repository
caption: Eight years on, the four-node network of late 1969 had grown to about sixty IMPs, including a satellite link to London and Norway. The map's own note warns that it shows only the 'host population ... according to the best information obtainable'.
